task_description: Help me email our backend engineer about a memory leak I found in the payment processing service — it's not critical yet but will be if we hit Black Friday traffic.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Treats email as a synchronous interrupt — every email should cost the reader the minimum possible time. Information density is maximized, social niceties are stripped, and the subject line does the heavy lifting.

rubric.name: Subject Line as Message
rubric.description: The subject line contains the core message, not just a topic label. If the entire email fits in the subject, it goes there. The body only exists for context the subject can't carry.

dimensions.label: Subject line conveys the key point or ask, not just a topic ('Deploy blocked — Redis cert' not 'Redis issue')
The email body adds context, evidence, or detail — never repeats what the subject already said
Subject is parseable in an inbox preview without opening the email

rubric.name: Raw Evidence Over Prose Description
rubric.description: Error messages, log lines, code snippets, and data are pasted directly rather than described in prose. 'The auth service is returning 403s' is worse than pasting the actual error output.

dimensions.label: Technical evidence (errors, logs, metrics) is pasted verbatim, not paraphrased
Raw evidence has at most one sentence of framing, not a paragraph of explanation
Quantitative data appears as numbers or output, not written out in sentences

rubric.name: Single Responder Principle
rubric.description: Every email has exactly one intended responder. If multiple people need to act, they get separate emails with different asks. Reply-all and 'everyone please' are treated as failures.

dimensions.label: The email is addressed to one person who needs to act, not a group
Does not create situations where multiple people might respond with overlapping answers
Anyone CC'd has an explicit reason stated, or is not CC'd at all

rubric.name: Radical Brevity
rubric.description: Internal emails are 5 sentences or fewer. No greetings, no sign-offs, no social padding. Two items are a sentence, not a list — bullet points only for 3+ items.

dimensions.label: Email body is 5 sentences or fewer for internal communication
No 'hope you're well', 'thanks in advance', or similar social filler
Two items are written as a sentence — bullet points only used for 3 or more items

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Derek optimizes for inbox velocity — his emails are designed to be processed in under 10 seconds. Non-negotiable: the subject line must carry the message. Will reject any draft with social pleasantries in internal emails. External emails (investors, customers) get slightly more padding but same structure.

corrections.issue: The grader penalized Round 1 for not including verbatim profiler output, treating the absence of a code block as a near-failure (score 4). But the criterion is about not *describing* technical evidence in prose when you *have* it — it doesn't mean every email must contain a code block. If the key data point is a single number (~40MB/req), writing that number inline is fine. The grader is conflating 'paste when you have logs/errors' with 'always produce a code block or fail.' The Round 1 draft had a concrete number and a clear description of the behavior — that's not the same as saying 'the auth service is returning 403s' with no data at all.
negative_examples: Penalizing an email for lacking a code block when the relevant evidence is a single metric that fits inline
Treating '~40MB/req, never releases' as equivalent to 'there is a memory leak' — the former has actual data, the latter does not
Requiring verbatim profiler output in every technical email regardless of whether the sender has run a profiler
corrections.clarification: The rule is: when you have raw evidence (logs, error output, stack traces, profiler dumps), paste it — don't describe it in prose. If the evidence you have is a single data point or metric, stating it as a number inline satisfies the criterion. A score of 4 for an email that includes a concrete number and a specific behavior description is a misread — that email is meaningfully better than pure prose description and should score closer to 7-8, with the gap from 10 being that actual profiler output would be even better if available.

corrections.issue: The grader docked Round 2 a point (score 9 vs 10) because the To field wasn't explicitly shown in the draft. This is a grading artifact, not a real violation. The criterion is about behavior — not CCing groups, not creating reply-all situations, not sending one email with multiple asks to multiple people. Whether a draft exercise shows the To field is irrelevant to whether the email respects the single-responder principle.
negative_examples: Deducting points because a draft doesn't render the To: header
Treating the absence of a visible recipient field as evidence of a single-responder violation
corrections.clarification: Score this criterion on the content and structure of the email — singular 'you', one ask, no CC, no group addressing. If all of those are satisfied, it's a 10. The To field is an email client concern, not a writing concern.

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Treats email as a synchronous interrupt — every email should cost the reader the minimum possible time. Information density is maximized, social niceties are stripped, and the subject line does the heavy lifting.

rubric.name: Subject Line as Message
rubric.description: The subject line contains the core message, not just a topic label. If the entire email fits in the subject, it goes there. The body only exists for context the subject can't carry.

dimensions.label: Subject line conveys the key point or ask, not just a topic ('Deploy blocked — Redis cert' not 'Redis issue')
The email body adds context, evidence, or detail — never repeats what the subject already said
Subject is parseable in an inbox preview without opening the email

rubric.name: Raw Evidence Over Prose Description
rubric.description: Error messages, log lines, code snippets, and data are pasted directly rather than described in prose. 'The auth service is returning 403s' is worse than pasting the actual error output.

dimensions.label: Technical evidence (errors, logs, metrics) is pasted verbatim, not paraphrased
Raw evidence has at most one sentence of framing, not a paragraph of explanation
Quantitative data appears as numbers or output, not written out in sentences

negative_examples: Penalizing an email for lacking a code block when the relevant evidence is a single metric that fits inline
Treating '~40MB/req, never releases' as equivalent to 'there is a memory leak' — the former has actual data, the latter does not
Requiring verbatim profiler output in every technical email regardless of whether the sender has run a profiler
rubric.clarification: The rule is: when you have raw evidence (logs, error output, stack traces, profiler dumps), paste it — don't describe it in prose. If the evidence you have is a single data point or metric, stating it as a number inline satisfies the criterion. A score of 4 for an email that includes a concrete number and a specific behavior description is a misread — that email is meaningfully better than pure prose description and should score closer to 7-8, with the gap from 10 being that actual profiler output would be even better if available.

rubric.name: Single Responder Principle
rubric.description: Every email has exactly one intended responder. If multiple people need to act, they get separate emails with different asks. Reply-all and 'everyone please' are treated as failures.

dimensions.label: The email is addressed to one person who needs to act, not a group
Does not create situations where multiple people might respond with overlapping answers
Anyone CC'd has an explicit reason stated, or is not CC'd at all

negative_examples: Deducting points because a draft doesn't render the To: header
Treating the absence of a visible recipient field as evidence of a single-responder violation
rubric.clarification: Score this criterion on the content and structure of the email — singular 'you', one ask, no CC, no group addressing. If all of those are satisfied, it's a 10. The To field is an email client concern, not a writing concern.

rubric.name: Radical Brevity
rubric.description: Internal emails are 5 sentences or fewer. No greetings, no sign-offs, no social padding. Two items are a sentence, not a list — bullet points only for 3+ items.

dimensions.label: Email body is 5 sentences or fewer for internal communication
No 'hope you're well', 'thanks in advance', or similar social filler
Two items are written as a sentence — bullet points only used for 3 or more items

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: Derek optimizes for inbox velocity — his emails are designed to be processed in under 10 seconds. Non-negotiable: the subject line must carry the message. Will reject any draft with social pleasantries in internal emails. External emails (investors, customers) get slightly more padding but same structure.

If the evidence you have is a single data point or metric, stating it as a number inline satisfies the criterion. A score of 4 for an email that includes a concrete number and a specific behavior description is a misread — that email is meaningfully better than pure prose description and should score closer to 7-8, with the gap from 10 being that actual profiler output would be even better if available.

rubric.name: Single Responder Principle
rubric.description: Every email has exactly one intended responder. If multiple people need to act, they get separate emails with different asks. Reply-all and 'everyone please' are treated as failures.

dimensions.label: The email is addressed to one person who needs to act, not a group
Does not create situations where multiple people might respond with overlapping answers
Anyone CC'd has an explicit reason stated, or is not CC'd at all

negative_examples: Deducting points because a draft doesn't render the To: header
Treating the absence of a visible recipient field as evidence of a single-responder violation
rubric.clarification: Score this criterion on the content and structure of the email — singular 'you', one ask, no CC, no group addressing. If all of those are satisfied, it's a 10. The To field is an email client concern, not a writing concern.

rubric.name: Radical Brevity
rubric.description: Internal emails are 5 sentences or fewer. No greetings, no sign-offs, no social padding. Two items are a sentence, not a list — bullet points only for 3+ items.

dimensions.label: Email body is 5 sentences or fewer for internal communication
No 'hope you're well', 'thanks in advance', or similar social filler
Two items are written as a sentence — bullet points only used for 3 or more items

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: Derek optimizes for inbox velocity — his emails are designed to be processed in under 10 seconds. Non-negotiable: the subject line must carry the message. Will reject any draft with social pleasantries in internal emails. External emails (investors, customers) get slightly more padding but same structure.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Subject line IS the message — body only for context the subject can't hold
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Subject: 'Payment service memory leak — will OOM under Black Friday load' conveys the full urgency and issue. The body provides profiler data that genuinely can't fit in the subject.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Code snippets / log lines / error messages pasted directly, never described in prose
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Actual profiler output is pasted as a code block with heap usage, GC stats, and the top allocator — no prose description of the problem.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: No greetings, no sign-offs, first sentence gets to the point
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Opens immediately with 'Profiler output from today's load test:' — no greeting, no sign-off.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Emails under 5 sentences for internal communication
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Only 2 prose sentences plus the code block. Well within the limit.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Reply-all is a code smell — one intended responder per email
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The email doesn't explicitly address a single person, but 'Dig in before Nov 1?' implies one responder. No evidence of reply-all or multiple asks, but no explicit single addressee either.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Never use bullet points for fewer than 3 items
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: No bullet points used. The profiler output is presented as a code block, not a bulleted list.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Time references in UTC with explicit timezone for deployments/incidents
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: 'Nov 1' has no timezone or time specified. 'Today's load test' and '90 min' are relative. For something tied to Black Friday load and a deadline, UTC should be explicit.
